---
title: Keys and Registry
---

A signature is only as meaningful as the binding between a key and a person. In Phase 1 that
binding is a software key and a flat file: enough to exercise every other part of the design, and
clearly labelled as not proving who signed. This page covers where keys live, what the registry
records and what changes when biometric signing arrives.


## Dev-Mode Keys

`sib keygen` creates an Ed25519 private key with the `cryptography` library and stores it under
`SIB_HOME` (`~/.sib` unless the variable is set):

```text
$SIB_HOME/dev-keys/alice@example.com#dev-2026-09.pem
```

The file is PKCS#8 PEM without a passphrase, written with mode `0600`. Characters outside
`A-Za-z0-9._@#-` in the key id are replaced with `_` in the file name. Every command that creates
or uses a dev key prints the same line to standard error:

```text
SIB DEV MODE: currently using software-only keys. Signatures only prove possession of the key file, not a verified human.
```

::: {.callout-important}
A dev key proves that whoever signed could read a file. It does not prove a person was present.
Dev mode exists so the rest of the system can be built and tested; enforced mode refuses dev keys
outright.
:::


## Key Identifiers

A key id (`kid`) names one enrolled key and appears in every block signed with it. The convention
is the signer id, a `#`, and a label:

```text
alice@example.com#dev-2026-09
alice@example.com#passkey-7c1e
```

The label distinguishes a person's keys from each other, so a dev key and a passkey can coexist and
either can be rotated. The verifier does not parse the label; it looks the whole `kid` up in the
registry and checks that the registry's signer matches the header's `iss`.


## Enrollment

Enrollment records a public key under a signer id. The usual path creates and enrolls in one step:

```bash
# Create a dev key and enroll it for alice
sib keygen --kid "alice@example.com#dev-2026-09" --enroll --signer alice@example.com
```

```text
SIB DEV MODE: currently using software-only keys. Signatures only prove possession of the key file, not a verified human.
dev key created for kid alice@example.com#dev-2026-09
public key: JmbApRbWb-3nVyk_H9vMHMId6bSA_znZfS2_aRnu5Hc
enrolled alice@example.com#dev-2026-09 for alice@example.com in /tmp/sib-doc-blocks/registry.json (dev mode, attestation_verified=false)
```

To enroll a public key produced elsewhere, use `sib enroll`:

`--signer ID`
: The signer's stable identifier (e.g., an email address).

`--kid KID`
: The key id, following the convention above.

`--public-key KEY`
: The raw public key, base64url without padding.

`--alg ALG`
: The signature algorithm (default: `EdDSA`).

`--dev`
: Mark the key as a dev key. Without it the key is enrolled in enforced mode, which in Phase 1 no
  signing path can use.

Enrolling a `kid` that already exists is an error; a key is never silently replaced.


## The Registry File

The registry is one JSON file at `$SIB_HOME/registry.json`:

```json
{
  "signers": [
    {
      "signer": "alice@example.com",
      "keys": [
        {
          "kid": "alice@example.com#dev-2026-09",
          "alg": "EdDSA",
          "public_key": "JmbApRbWb-3nVyk_H9vMHMId6bSA_znZfS2_aRnu5Hc",
          "mode": "dev",
          "enrolled_at": "2026-09-13T14:06:30Z",
          "attestation_verified": false,
          "attestation": {},
          "revoked": false
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

Each key carries:

`alg`, `public_key`
: What the verifier needs to check a signature. The verifier also requires the header's `alg` to
  match this entry.

`mode`
: `dev` or `enforced`. A key enrolled in dev mode fails with `dev_key_in_enforced_mode` when the
  verifier runs in enforced mode, whatever the block's own header says.

`enrolled_at`
: When the entry was made, RFC 3339 in UTC.

`attestation_verified`, `attestation`
: Whether the enrollment carried attestation that the verifier checked, and what it said. Always
  false and empty for dev keys. This is the field that will separate "hardware backing verified"
  from "hardware backing assumed" once biometric keys exist.

`revoked`
: Honored by the verifier (status `revoked`), but no command sets it yet.

The registry is the stand-in for the external directory that maps signer keys to people, which the
project treats as out of scope. It is a flat file so that it stays easy to inspect and to ship with
a demo; it is not access-controlled beyond file permissions.


## Dev Mode and Enforced Mode

The verifier's mode comes from the harness (`SIB_MODE`, default `dev` in Phase 1) and is recorded
in every manifest. The two modes differ in three places:

- **Dev keys**: accepted in dev mode, refused in enforced mode.

- **Audience**: a block with no `aud` is accepted in dev mode and is `audience_mismatch` in
  enforced mode.

- **Warnings**: dev mode prints its warning on every operation. Enforced mode is silent.

Nothing else changes, so a session can be developed in dev mode and switched to enforced mode once
a real key is enrolled.


## What Phase 2 Changes

Phase 2 replaces the dev key with a WebAuthn passkey (Touch ID on macOS first), as planned in
`plans/phase-2-biometric-signing.md`. The plan is stated here so the registry format is read with
it in mind:

- Enrollment happens through a local web page that calls `navigator.credentials.create` with user
  verification required. The registry entry gets `alg: ES256-webauthn`, the credential's public
  key, the authenticator's AAGUID and whatever attestation the authenticator returned.

- `attestation_verified` becomes true only when the attestation format could be checked against a
  vendor root. Apple platform passkeys often return no attestation, in which case the AAGUID is
  self-reported and the field stays false.

- Signing places the SHA-256 of the signing input in the WebAuthn challenge. The verifier
  recomputes it, checks the origin and RP ID, requires the user-verification flag and verifies the
  ES256 signature with the enrolled key.

- The user-verification flag covers PIN and password as well as biometrics, so "biometric" is
  enforced by an allowlist of biometric-capable authenticators rather than proven by the
  signature. That limit is documented rather than hidden.

Until then, every block is a dev block, and every registry entry says so.
